new_statements.quote: 9. Ton und Nachdruck. — In Sammlung C ist meist die letzte Silbe durch den Akut als betont bezeichnet, seltener die vorletzte. Höchst wahrscheinlich ist aber auch im Adele die Unterscheidung von hohem und tiefem Ton mindestens so wichtig für die Bedeutung der Wörter, als die Bezeichnung der Nachdrucksilbe. Der Nachdruck fällt oft mit dem ersten hohen Ton eines Wortes zusammen, kann aber auch auf tieftoniger Silbe liegen.
new_statements.translation: 9. Tone and stress. — In collection C [Conradt's word list] it is mostly the last syllable that is marked with the acute as stressed, more rarely the penultimate. Most probably, however, in Adele too the distinction of high and low tone is at least as important for the meaning of words as the marking of the stressed syllable. The stress often coincides with the first high tone of a word, but can also lie on a low-toned syllable.
new_statements.citation: Christaller, J. G. 1895. Die Adelesprache im Togogebiet. Zeitschrift für afrikanische und oceanische Sprachen 1: 16-33.

new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record (adel1244 has no catalog record and no stress statement held by the project). Compatible with the sources already read: Rongier 1998 front matter 'TONS: 2 tons : bas, haut' matches Christaller's high/low-tone conjecture; Westermann 1922 and the Rongier dictionaries are silent on stress, so Christaller 1895 §9 is the only located statement about word prominence in Adele (mostly final, sometimes penult, per Conradt's marks), and it is explicitly tentative.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Christaller (working from three second-hand word lists, chiefly Conradt's c. 1100-word collection 'C') reports that the transcriber's acute/stress mark falls mostly on the LAST syllable of the word, less often on the penult; he adds that Adele very probably distinguishes high and low tone lexically (at least as important for meaning as stress placement), that the stress ('Nachdruck') often coincides with the first high tone of a word but may also sit on a low-toned syllable. Elsewhere he assumes tone distinguishes homophonous verbs (p. 30) and probably marks negation as in Twi (p. 31). Net: a tone language (high/low, inferred) with word prominence reported as predominantly final, sometimes penultimate, in the 1892-93 transcriptions; no fixed rule is asserted and Christaller himself flags that the acute marks may partly encode high tone rather than stress.
new_statements.exceptions: 'seltener die vorletzte' (penultimate stress in a minority of items in list C); stress can lie on a low-toned syllable; prefixes are unstressed 'Nebensilben' (p. 22 §19) and very short vowels before r/l may drop (p. 19 §7), implying prominence on the root syllable rather than the prefix; all statements are hedged as based on Europeans' first transcriptions ('oft nur annähernd richtig').
new_statements.identity_note: Adele as recorded at and around the German station Bismarckburg (Adele hill country, today's Togo-Ghana border) in 1884 (David Asante, numerals + 17 words), 1890-91 (station head, c. 300 words/100 sentences) and 1892-93 (Conradt, c. 1100 words); Christaller never heard the language himself and normalises the three transcriptions; no dialect (Upper/Lower Adele) is distinguished, though he notes B/C variation (e.g. egera ~ eyera 'sheep').
